speaker_role: independent counselors (two Quad Education admissions consultants; one previously at Columbia/PhD program, one Harvard grad with prior work at Washington University in St. Louis)
commercial_incentive: yes; webinar run by a paid consulting firm (Quad Education Group), which repeatedly promotes booking a 'Quad counselor' consultation
key_insights: Defines reach (under 20% admit chance for the student's stats), target (20-80%), and safety (over 80%) schools, recommending roughly 10-15 total schools rather than 20-40

A 'safety school' can still deny an over-qualified applicant via yield protection, so recommends targeting specific competitive programs within safety schools (e.g., honors college, pharmacy) rather than assuming blanket safety
Recommends using each target school's Common Data Set to see the actual 25th-75th percentile GPA/test-score bands, rather than relying on rough published ranges

Test-optional policies were applied inconsistently in the cycle discussed: some schools appeared to expect submission if a score was near/above the 50th percentile of admits, and AP/IB scores gained added weight when SAT/ACT was withheld
Early Decision I (November) and ED II (January) are explained as fully binding except for inadequate financial aid, and are recommended for a 'realistic reach' rather than a maximal reach

High schools' own historical admissions data (via Naviance, Scoir, Maia Learning) showing which past applicants with specific stats got into which schools is highlighted as uniquely useful, school-specific data
specific_numbers_or_facts: Recommended list size: 10-15 schools total, versus some students applying to 20-40
Application fees cited around $85 or more per school
notable_or_distinctive: unusually concrete, repeated emphasis on using each school's Common Data Set and the applicant's own high school's historical Naviance/Scoir data as the primary quantitative list-building tools
reliability_notes: transcript is a roughly one-hour sales webinar from a paid consulting firm with an embedded Q&A; test-optional/AP-weighting claims reflect one specific recent cycle and are dated; consultants explicitly decline to give individualized stats advice on air, steering listeners toward paid consultations
